channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: Sleeping on it improves your problem-solving abilities.
item.description: A 2004 study found that participants who slept were significantly more likely to gain insight into a hidden mathematical rule than those who remained awake.

item.title: Your name influences your career choices.
item.description: Research in the early 2000s suggested a correlation between initials and career choice, but this has been largely debunked as an artifact of confounders.

item.title: Music tempo changes how you shop.
item.description: A 1986 study found that stores playing slower music saw significantly higher sales than those playing faster tempos.

item.title: Ambient noise levels determine your creativity.
item.description: A 2012 study found that moderate levels of ambient noise boost abstract thinking compared to total silence.

item.title: Standing tall makes you believe your own thoughts more.
item.description: A 2009 study found that participants who maintained an upright posture reported more confidence in their own written thoughts.

item.title: Expressing gratitude consistently rewires your daily outlook.
item.description: A 2003 study showed that writing about things you are grateful for increases well-being compared to focusing on daily hassles.

item.title: A fake smile can change your mood.
item.description: A 1988 study claimed that participants rated cartoons as funnier when holding a pen in their teeth, but these findings have not been replicated in subsequent large-scale research.

item.title: Red colors subtly kill your performance on tests.
item.description: A 2007 study by Elliot et al. in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General found that viewing the color red before an exam can result in statistically significant performance decrements, but these are small in magnitude, not a 20% reduction.

item.title: Holding a warm drink makes you perceive others as kinder.
item.description: In a 2008 study by Williams and Bargh, participants holding a warm coffee cup judged a stranger as having a warmer personality than those holding iced coffee, though subsequent attempts to replicate these findings have failed.

item.title: You forget your intentions when you walk through doorways.
item.description: A 2011 study found that entering a new room significantly decreases your ability to recall information from the previous one.

item.title: You are driven either by hope or caution.
item.description: Regulatory focus theory identifies two different motivational systems: a promotion focus on achievement and a prevention focus on safety.

item.title: You fail because you trust your first instinct.
item.description: The Cognitive Reflection Test shows that people often fail simple logic puzzles by relying on intuitive, incorrect answers.

item.title: Your judgment is relative to what came before.
item.description: The sequential contrast effect shows that your evaluation of an object changes based on the quality of the item immediately preceding it.

item.title: You only act when the result seems possible.
item.description: Expectancy theory states that motivation is the multiplicative product of three factors: expectancy (that effort leads to performance), instrumentality (that performance leads to a reward), and valence (the value the individual places on that reward).

item.title: You cannot ignore the meaning of a word.
item.description: The Stroop effect demonstrates that you are slower at identifying the ink color of a word that names a different color.

item.title: You feel worse when your friend succeeds.
item.description: Self-evaluation maintenance theory explains why your self-esteem drops when a close friend performs exceptionally well.

item.title: You prefer a smaller reward that is certain.
item.description: Research shows people systematically choose lower-value, certain rewards over higher-value options involving uncertainty.

item.title: Warm coffee makes you judge people more kindly.
item.description: A 2008 study reported this finding, but the effect has not been successfully replicated in later research.

item.title: You are more likely to trust a stranger if they share your birthday.
item.description: Implicit egotism is a controversial hypothesis proposing a subconscious preference for self-associated stimuli, but it has not been conclusively proven or reliably replicated.

item.title: You mistake the ease of recalling a reason for the validity of that reason.
item.description: The availability heuristic leads you to treat information that is easier to remember as more important or frequent.

item.title: Your brain prefers to categorize people by race to process information faster.
item.description: People are generally more accurate at recognizing faces of their own race, a phenomenon known as the cross-race effect or own-race bias.

item.title: You believe your thoughts are more transparent to others than they really are.
item.description: The illusion of transparency leads you to overestimate how well others can read your emotional state.

item.title: A moment of awe makes you feel like time is slowing down.
item.description: Experiencing awe expands your perception of time, leaving you feeling like you have more of it.

item.title: You assume a name is famous simply because you saw it earlier.
item.description: The false fame effect leads people to misattribute familiarity to celebrity status.

item.title: A smaller gift can feel more valuable than a larger one.
item.description: The less-is-better effect, described by Christopher Hsee in 1998, demonstrates that individuals often value smaller sets of high-quality items more than larger sets containing those same items plus inferior ones when evaluated separately.

item.title: You lose cognitive precision when performing two tasks simultaneously.
item.description: Cognitive load theory shows that your working memory has a limited capacity for information processing.

item.title: Your brain cannot process two independent tasks at once.
item.description: The psychological refractory period causes a delay in reaction to a second stimulus if it arrives during the processing of the first.

item.title: You process sentences faster when they match your physical movement.
item.description: The action-sentence compatibility effect demonstrates that manual reaction times are faster when the sentence describes movement in that direction.

item.title: You recall information best in the same environment you learned it.
item.description: The encoding specificity principle suggests that memory retrieval is aided by cues present during the initial learning event.

item.title: You prioritize trivial tasks because they offer immediate completion.
item.description: The mere urgency effect shows people choose tasks with shorter deadlines over tasks with higher rewards.

item.title: You react faster when your hand matches the stimulus position.
item.description: The Simon effect shows that response times are faster when the stimulus location corresponds to the response location.

item.title: You unconsciously copy the sentence structure of people you speak to.
item.description: Syntactic priming makes you more likely to repeat the grammatical structure of the sentence you just heard.

item.title: Your brain ignores facial details when a face is upside down.
item.description: The Thatcher effect causes inverted faces to appear normal despite grotesque distortions in the eyes and mouth.

item.title: Your attention is wired to follow where others look.
item.description: The gaze cueing effect shows that human attention shifts automatically to follow another person's eyes.

item.title: Your brain actively blocks information you recently chose to ignore.
item.description: Negative priming demonstrates that identifying a target is slower if the item was previously ignored.

item.title: Your brain treats abstract ideas as physical weight.
item.description: Participants holding a heavy clipboard rated job applicants as having more 'serious' and 'significant' personalities.

item.title: You fix mistakes faster when you feel certain.
item.description: Participants were more likely to correct an error if they were 'highly confident' that the wrong answer was actually correct.

item.title: Your environment shapes how you perceive basic lines.
item.description: In a study of 14 societies, people living in 'carpentered' environments were more susceptible to the Müller-Lyer illusion.

item.title: You link abstract sounds to specific physical shapes.
item.description: Research by Ramachandran and Hubbard (2001) reported that 95% of participants associated the names as described, but this effect is not universal across all cultures.

item.title: Your perception of reality shifts to match others.
item.description: In 1935, Sherif found that people converge on a shared estimate when viewing a stationary dot of light in a dark room.

item.title: You hear sounds differently based on lip movement.
item.description: In a 1976 study, participants reported hearing 'da' when a speaker’s mouth showed 'ga' but the audio played 'ba'.

item.title: You change your opinion to avoid social isolation.
item.description: In a 1951 experiment, 74% of participants went along with an obviously incorrect group judgment at least once.

item.title: You work harder for rewards you did not earn.
item.description: In the 2011 'IKEA Effect' study, participants were willing to pay significantly more—in one experiment, 63% more—for products they assembled themselves compared to those assembled by others.

item.title: You interpret your own physiological arousal incorrectly every day.
item.description: A 1962 study (Schachter and Singer) proposed that physiological arousal is labeled as an emotion (specifically anger or euphoria in their experiments) based on social context.

item.title: You view your past self as a complete stranger.
item.description: A 2009 study found that brain activity patterns when thinking about your future self resemble those for thinking about a different person.

item.title: You consistently overestimate your ability to control external events.
item.description: When an outcome is preceded by your own action, even if it is unrelated, you feel a 'sense of agency' that causes you to believe you caused it.

item.title: You interpret ambiguity based on your current physical comfort.
item.description: Hard chairs make people more 'stubborn' and 'unyielding' during negotiations compared to soft seating.

item.title: You unconsciously adjust your gait to match others.
item.description: When walking with a partner, your stride frequency naturally synchronizes within minutes to match theirs.

item.title: You can misidentify the source of your own thoughts.
item.description: Cryptomnesia occurs when you mistake a forgotten memory for a brand-new, original idea.

item.title: You can temporarily destroy the meaning of any word.
item.description: Semantic satiation is triggered by the high frequency of word repetition over a short period, rather than a specific 30-second threshold.
